name: Periodic Table Trends
description: Place elements by metallic character and by the family whose properties they share.

facets.label: Metallic Character
facets.prompt: Is {entity} a metal, a metalloid or a nonmetal?

groups.label: Metal
groups.hint: Conducts well, loses electrons, forms basic oxides

groups.label: Metalloid
groups.hint: Sits on the staircase; semiconducting, intermediate behaviour

groups.label: Nonmetal
groups.hint: Poor conductor, gains or shares electrons, forms acidic oxides

groups.label: Alkali Metal
groups.hint: Group 1; one valence electron, violently reactive with water

groups.label: Alkaline Earth Metal
groups.hint: Group 2; two valence electrons, reactive but less so than group 1

groups.label: Transition Metal
groups.hint: d-block; variable oxidation states, often coloured compounds

groups.label: Halogen
groups.hint: Group 17; one electron short of a full shell, strong oxidisers

groups.label: Noble Gas
groups.hint: Group 18; full valence shell, almost no reactivity

groups.label: Metalloid
groups.hint: Along the staircase between metals and nonmetals

explain.character: Lithium is a soft, conductive group 1 metal, despite being light enough to float on water.
explain.family: It heads group 1 with a single valence electron, so it reacts with water to give a hydroxide and hydrogen gas.

explain.character: A group 1 metal, and one that must be stored under oil because it oxidises on contact with air.
explain.family: Reactivity increases down group 1, so potassium reacts with water far more violently than lithium does.

explain.character: A structural metal, light and conductive, used in alloys where weight matters.
explain.family: Group 2 with two valence electrons, forming Mg²⁺; it is not an alkali metal despite the similar-sounding name.

explain.character: A dense, reactive metal that tarnishes quickly in air.
explain.family: Group 2, sitting below magnesium and calcium, and reactive enough to be handled under oil like the alkali metals.

explain.character: A strong, corrosion-resistant metal, protected by a tough oxide layer.
explain.family: A d-block element with several oxidation states, most commonly +4 as in TiO₂.

explain.character: A metal used to galvanise steel, sacrificing itself to corrosion first.
explain.family: It sits in the d-block, though its filled d shell and single +2 state make it behave less typically than iron or copper.

explain.character: A diatomic gas that gains electrons rather than losing them, forming acidic oxides.
explain.family: Group 17, one electron short of a full shell, which makes it a powerful oxidising agent.

explain.character: A nonmetal despite its metallic sheen as a solid; it sublimes to a violet vapour.
explain.family: Group 17, but the least reactive common halogen, since the larger atom holds an added electron less tightly.

explain.character: A nonmetal gas, and the third most abundant component of dry air.
explain.family: Group 18 with a full valence shell, which is why it is used as an inert shield in welding.

explain.character: A nonmetal gas, monatomic and colourless under ordinary conditions.
explain.family: Group 18; heavier noble gases are not perfectly inert, and krypton does form compounds such as KrF₂ under force.

explain.character: It has a metallic lustre but conducts only when doped or heated, which is the defining metalloid behaviour.
explain.family: It sits on the staircase between aluminium and phosphorus, and that intermediate position is what makes semiconductors possible.

explain.character: Its grey allotrope looks and conducts somewhat like a metal, while it forms covalent compounds like a nonmetal.
explain.family: A staircase element in group 15, used as a dopant in semiconductors for exactly that intermediate character.
